title: Performance Fundamentals
description: Understand what makes Git slow and the strategies for keeping repositories fast.

data.text: Git performance issues typically stem from three sources: a large number of files, a long history with many commits, and large binary files. Understanding which factor is causing the slowdown tells you which optimization to apply: shallow clones, partial clones, sparse checkout, or Git LFS.

Before optimizing, measure where the time is spent. Use git count-objects to see object count and disk usage. Use git rev-list --count to see total commits. Use time git <command> to measure wall-clock time.

data.title: Measure repository size and object count
data.code:
# Count loose objects and disk usage
git count-objects -vH

# Output:
# count: 15234
# size: 238.50 MiB
# in-pack: 48201
# pack-size: 312.34 MiB

# Count total commits
git rev-list --count HEAD

# Time a Git command
time git log --oneline --all > /dev/null

# Check disk usage of .git directory
du -sh .git

data.title: Git performance bottlenecks
items: **Too many files**: Git must stat every file on checkout
**Too much history**: Full clones download the entire commit history
**Large binaries**: Git stores every version of every binary, bloating the repo
**Too many refs**: Large numbers of branches and tags slow down many commands
**Unpacked objects**: Loose objects are slower to read than packed objects

data.text: Match the optimization to the bottleneck. If history is the problem, use shallow clones. If disk usage is the problem, pack loose objects. If binary files are the problem, use Git LFS. If you only need part of the repo, use sparse checkout.

rows: git lfs install + git lfs track

data.text: Over time, Git accumulates many loose objects — individual files in .git/objects/. These are slower to read and take more disk space than packed objects. Run git gc to pack loose objects and remove unreachable objects.

data.title: Pack loose objects with git gc
data.code:
# Run garbage collection to pack objects
git gc --aggressive

# This:
# 1. Packs loose objects into .git/objects/pack/
# 2. Removes unreachable objects
# 3. Prunes reflog entries older than 90 days
# 4. Optimizes the repository for speed

# Verify the result
git count-objects -vH

data.title: Git runs gc automatically
data.text: Git runs gc automatically when loose objects exceed certain thresholds. You rarely need to run it manually unless you notice a sudden slowdown after a large operation like a rebase or filter-branch.
In CI environments, every second counts. Use shallow clones or partial clones to reduce the data transferred during checkout.

data.title: Shallow clone in CI
data.code:
# GitHub Actions: shallow clone
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
- uses: actions/checkout@v4
  with:
    fetch-depth: 1  # shallow clone

# GitLab CI: shallow clone
# .gitlab-ci.yml
gitlab_ci:
  script:
    - git clone --depth 1 https://gitlab.com/example/project.git

# Without fetch-depth, actions/checkout fetches full history
# which can add 10-30 seconds for large repositories

items.question: Does git gc affect the working directory?
items.answer: No. git gc only modifies .git/objects/ and other internal files. It does not touch your working directory or staging area.

items.question: Can I run git gc on a bare repository?
items.answer: Yes. git gc is often run on bare repositories (shared remotes) to keep them fast. Use git gc --aggressive for deep optimization.

items.question: Does shallow clone support pushing?
items.answer: No. Shallow clones cannot push because they do not have the full history. Use a full clone for branches you need to push from.

items.question: How often should I run git gc?
items.answer: Let Git run it automatically. Git runs gc when the number of loose objects exceeds the threshold (default 6700). You can also set git config gc.auto to control this.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Measure first: use git count-objects, git rev-list --count, and time
Bottlenecks are history, files, binaries, or refs
git gc packs loose objects and removes unreachable data
Use shallow clones in CI to reduce checkout time
Match the optimization strategy to the specific bottleneck
